paragraphs.heading: Who he was
paragraphs.text: Martin Luther, who lived from 1483 to 1546, was a German priest, theologian, writer, hymn composer and professor, and once an Augustinian friar. He was the key figure of the Protestant Reformation, and his ideas about God and faith are the foundation of Lutheranism. He is counted among the most influential people in the history of the West and of Christianity.

paragraphs.heading: Growing up
paragraphs.text: Luther was born in Eisleben on 10 November 1483, the eldest son of Hans Luder. His father was set on him becoming a lawyer and sent him to Latin schools in Mansfeld, Magdeburg and Eisenach. Luther later likened those schools to purgatory and hell. At 17, in 1501, he went to the University of Erfurt, and he earned his master's degree in 1505. He then began studying law as his father wished, but quit almost at once, feeling that law was an uncertain career.

paragraphs.heading: From law to the monastery
paragraphs.text: Seeking certainty about life, Luther turned to theology and philosophy. Philosophy let him down: it gave confidence in reason but none about loving God, which mattered more to him. He came to believe people could know God only through God revealing himself, so scripture grew ever more important to him. Two stories explain his sudden choice to become a monk. In one, he was shaken by the sudden death of a university friend; in the other, lightning struck near him during a storm on 2 July 1505 as he rode back to university.

paragraphs.heading: Breaking with Rome
paragraphs.text: Luther was ordained a priest in 1507. He came to reject several Catholic teachings and practices, above all on indulgences and the power of the pope. In 1517 he wrote the Ninety-five Theses, which opened a debate across many countries. In 1520 Pope Leo X ordered him to take back all his writings; Luther refused and was excommunicated in January 1521. Later that year Emperor Charles V declared him an outlaw at the Diet of Worms, and he was still excommunicated when he died in 1546.

paragraphs.heading: What he taught
paragraphs.text: Luther taught that justification cannot be earned by anything people do, intend or deserve. Instead, he preached, it comes only as a free gift of God's grace, received through faith in Jesus. Good works still mattered: he saw them as the necessary fruit of a living faith and part of sanctification. He also held that the Bible alone reveals God's truth about the Gospel, which challenged the authority of the pope and bishops.

paragraphs.heading: Bible, hymns and marriage
paragraphs.text: Luther's German translation of the Bible, from 1534, put it within far easier reach of ordinary believers and deeply shaped both the Church and German culture. His translation helped form a standard German language and influenced the English Tyndale Bible. His hymns shaped how Protestant churches sing. By marrying Katharina von Bora, a former nun, he set a pattern that let Protestant clergy marry.

paragraphs.heading: A darker legacy
paragraphs.text: In 1523 Luther wrote that Jesus was born a Jew, and he discouraged mistreating Jews while hoping to convert them. As the Reformation grew, he lost hope of mass conversion, and as his health failed he grew far harsher toward Jews. He called for Jews to be expelled and their synagogues burned. He did not call for Jews to be killed, but some historians argue his words fed antisemitism in Germany and, centuries later, the rise of the Nazi Party.
